papers.title: Repeated sleep-medication reporting patterns and cognitive change in HRS and SHARE
papers.abstract: Background: Self-reported sleep-medication use has been inconsistently linked to cognitive decline, largely because sleep disturbances, affective symptoms, and treatment transitions co-evolve over time. Moreover, whether repeated sleep-medication reports across consecutive survey waves follow a monotonic dose-response gradient with subsequent cognitive aging remains unclear. We evaluated baseline, two-wave, and three-wave longitudinal patterns of sleep-medication reporting in relation to cognitive trajectories across two large aging cohorts in the United States and Europe. Methods: We analyzed population-based data from adults aged >=50 years in the US Health and Retirement Study (HRS) and the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE). First, we examined associations between baseline sleep-medication use and longitudinal changes in standardized global cognition and memory scores (Analysis 1: HRS n = 16,323; SHARE n = 41,453). Second, we conducted a prespecified two-wave landmark analysis classifying participants by reported sleep-medication use across two consecutive visits (HRS waves 11-12; SHARE waves 4-5) as 0, 1, or 2 use-positive visits, and by reporting sequence (00, 01, 10, and 11), with cognitive trajectories modeled from the second visit onward (Analysis 2: HRS n = 13,915; SHARE n = 29,214). Linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts and slopes adjusted for baseline sociodemographic, lifestyle, and clinical covariates and all covariate-by-time interactions. Third, we extended the landmark window to three consecutive visits (HRS waves 11-13, 2012-2016; SHARE waves 6-8, 2015-2020) to separate sustained from transient reporting, adjusting for interview mode and testing equivalence of sustained use to non-use (Analysis 3: HRS n = 12,310; SHARE n = 24,692). Results: In baseline analyses, sleep-medication use was associated with modestly faster decline in global cognition (HRS: beta = -0.0060 SD/year, 95% CI -0.0103 to -0.0017; SHARE: beta = -0.0034 SD/year, 95% CI -0.0070 to 0.0002) and memory (HRS: beta = -0.0062 SD/year, 95% CI -0.0115 to -0.0009; SHARE: beta = -0.0037 SD/year, 95% CI -0.0074 to 0.0001). papers.title: Perioperative non-invasive brain stimulation for the prevention of postoperative delirium: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
papers.abstract: BackgroundPostoperative delirium is a common perioperative complication. Early randomised trials suggested that non-invasive brain stimulation may reduce postoperative delirium, whereas the recent MODEST trial found no preventive benefit. We synthesised the randomised evidence for perioperative non-invasive brain stimulation. MethodsWe searched eight bibliographic databases and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to 30 September 2026 for randomised controlled trials of perioperative non-invasive brain stimulation in adults undergoing surgery. The primary outcome was postoperative delirium. Random-effects meta-analyses estimated risk ratios (RRs), mean differences, or standardised mean differences. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 and certainty of evidence using GRADE. ResultsNine trials contributed data from 1451 participants. Postoperative delirium occurred in 72 of 750 participants receiving active stimulation and 166 of 701 controls (RR 0.41, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.31-0.56; I2=24.7%; moderate-certainty evidence). Estimates also favoured stimulation for hypoactive and hyperactive delirium, but not clearly for mixed delirium. Pain, anxiety, and sleep outcomes favoured stimulation but were highly heterogeneous and supported by very-low-certainty evidence. Length of hospital stay was not reduced. Adverse events could not be pooled because reporting was incomplete and inconsistent. ConclusionsPerioperative non-invasive brain stimulation may reduce postoperative delirium, but the evidence does not establish a class effect or support routine clinical use. Geographical concentration, methodological concerns, heterogeneous stimulation protocols, and discordance with the MODEST trial warrant independent multicentre sham-controlled trials. PROSPERO registrationCRD420261522168

papers.title: A Local Enrichment Computational Framework to Identify Disease-Enriched Physical Activity Patterns
papers.abstract: Wearable accelerometers enable continuous monitoring of physical activity (PA), yet conventional summary measures and population-wide clustering approaches may overlook disease-associated behavioral heterogeneity. Here we introduce LocPA, a computational framework that identifies disease-enriched PA patterns through confounder-adjusted activity profiling, similarity network construction, local disease-enrichment testing and community detection. Applying LocPA to 24-hour accelerometry profiles from the UK Biobank, we identified two recurring PA phenotypes across six diseases spanning cardiometabolic, neurological, psychiatric, renal and cardiovascular conditions: a low-activity phenotype characterized by reduced daytime activity and a sleep-disrupted phenotype characterized by reduced daytime and elevated nocturnal activity. In hypertension and diabetes, the sleep-disrupted phenotype was associated with greater disease burden and less favorable clinical and metabolic profiles, differences not consistently captured by conventional PA summary measures. LocPA also identified disease-specific temporal patterns, particularly in Parkinsons disease. Analyses in an independent National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey cohort supported the recurrence of hypertension- and diabetes-enriched patterns across populations and accelerometry measurements. LocPA provides a flexible, disease-driven approach for uncovering clinically relevant temporal PA patterns, with potential applications in disease risk characterization and personalized behavioral interventions.

papers.title: BioLT: Streaming Biosignal Modeling
papers.abstract: Clinical biosignals such as ECG, PPG, and EEG are increasingly acquired as hours-long streams from bedside monitors and wearables, yet existing analysis pipelines almost universally operate on isolated short windows of around 10 seconds and cannot process the long, irregular, frequently interrupted signals. We introduce BioLT, a streaming decoder-only framework for long-context biosignal modeling that turns any window-level feature extractor or pretrained biosignal foundation model into a streaming model. BioLT combines (i) a discontinuity-aware encoding that exposes the inter-window elapsed time as an explicit input channel, so that the decoder can learn to model these gaps as clinically meaningful information, and (ii) a fixed-size compressed memory bank supervised with cumulative summary statistics, which keeps both training and inference linear in the recording length while preserving long-range context. We evaluate on CPSC-2021, VitalDB, MC-MED, and CHB-MIT for arrhythmia, sepsis, and seizure detection and for forecasting up to 20 minutes ahead, using domain features and embeddings from six biosignal foundation models. Across 21 dataset-feature settings, BioLT achieves the highest detection AUROC in 15 and the highest 20-minute forecasting AUROC in 13 settings, and shows consistent performance gains over state-of-the-art snapshot foundation-model embeddings. These highlight the importance of modeling how streaming biosignal representations evolve over time, beyond improving window-level representations alone.

papers.title: Feasibility of Vibrotactile P50 Sensory-Gating Assessment Using Portable EEG
papers.abstract: Sensory gating (SG), most commonly quantified using the auditory P50 event-related potential elicited by a paired "double-click" paradigm, is a well-established biomarker of early sensory inhibition that reflects the brain's ability to suppress responses to repetitive sensory input. Although auditory SG paradigms have been widely used in both research and clinical settings, they impose an unavoidable auditory load and are generally limited to controlled laboratory environments, reducing their suitability for ecological monitoring and applications in which auditory resources must remain available. This study evaluated the feasibility of a portable vibrotactile sensory-gating system designed to assess inhibitory processing without engaging the auditory or visual modalities. Fifteen healthy adult participants completed both auditory and vibrotactile paired-stimulus conditions using a within-subject experimental design. Vibrotactile stimuli were delivered through transducers positioned on the volar surface of the forearm while electroencephalographic (EEG) activity was recorded using a 32-channel Emotiv EPOC Flex system. Event-related responses were extracted and analyzed using conventional sensory-gating metrics to enable direct comparison between modalities. Vibrotactile stimulation elicited time-locked P50 responses with attenuation of S2 relative to S1. Mean S2/S1 ratios were 0.521 +- 0.041 for the auditory condition and 0.524 +- 0.064 for the vibrotactile condition. The paired difference was 0.0029 (95% CI, -0.0221 to 0.0279), t(14) = 0.249, p = 0.807, dz = 0.064. No statistically significant difference was detected between modalities in this sample. These group-level findings support further evaluation of portable vibrotactile P50 measurement.

papers.title: Optimisation of and mechanisms behind neural distortion responses obtained with cochlear-implant stimulation by interleaved pulse trains
papers.abstract: Purpose: We investigated the mechanisms behind the generation of Neural Distortion Responses (NDRs) measured with electroencephalography when interleaving amplitude-modulated (AM) pulse trains in cochlear implant (CI) users. Methods: Previous experiments measured NDRs using interleaved pulse trains in which odd- and even-numbered pulses were respectively modulated at F1 and F2 Hz, where F1=2*F2/3 and F1{approx}80Hz. Experiment 1 separated quadratic and cubic distortion products using a relationship of F1 and F2 such that F1 = (2*F2/3)+2. Experiment 2 retained the original F1=2*F2/3 relationship but shifted the starting AM phase of F2 relative to that of F1. Experiment 3 simultaneously separated the quadratic and cubic distortion products and varied the relative phase of F1 and F2. Experiment 4 flipped the leading polarity of the second pulse in each pulse-pair such that the central phase of the resulting pseudo-triphasic pulses was anodic. All experiments were conducted with Cochlear CI users and interpreted using two computational models of the electrically stimulated auditory nerve. Results: Both quadratic (QDR) and cubic distortion products (CDR) were observed. Varying relative AM phase had an effect on NDR amplitudes, with the largest amplitude when maxima of the 2 AM patterns were aligned. Stimulating with an anodic central phase within the AM pulse pairs resulted in stronger responses for 4 of 9 CI users. Computational modelling suggested a stronger role for refractoriness than for facilitation in generating the NDR, but failed to fully account for the effect of flipping the polarity. Conclusion: NDRs consist of both quadratic and cubic components, and are greatest when maxima of the F1 and F2 pulse trains align. Refractoriness is likely more important than facilitation for generating the NDR.

papers.title: Polygenic Prediction of Depression Liability Reveals Broad Genetic Associations Across Development, Families, and Populations
papers.abstract: Polygenic prediction of depression is limited by the depth of depression phenotyping available at biobank scale as well as sample size. Here we develop a depression score combining information from depression and genetically correlated psychiatric traits using phenotype reconstruction, multi-trait genetic integration and Bayesian effect estimation. Compared with the strongest publicly available depression-only score (Psychiatric Genomics Consortium 2025, excluding 23andMe), the liability-R2 for depression in UK Biobank rose by 49.7% and within-family standardized associations with latent internalizing were up to 54% larger. Across 2,328 childhood and adolescent outcomes in the ABCD study, the association profile of the integrated score was almost identical to that of the depression-only score (r = 0.99), while being uniformly stronger. 1,494 outcomes related to mood, behavior, social functioning, hobbies and sleep were associated with the score -- 423 of them within-family. In ABCD, adolescents in the highest score decile were 3.5 times as likely as those in the lowest decile to report suicidal thoughts by age 14 (23% versus 7%) and 1.9 times as likely to report nicotine or cannabis use by age 17 (47% versus 25%). In adults, the score predicted worse general health, chronic pain, and life dissatisfaction. Associations with psychiatric symptoms were substantially stronger in girls than in boys (boys' coefficients 0.68 times girls'), particularly for girl-typical symptoms, and showed no moderation by household resources, hardship or deprivation that remained significant after correction for multiple testing. Prediction was attenuated in line with genetic distance from training data for Hispanic and African American children. Depression prediction can thus be strengthened substantially by integrating the internalizing spectrum, without detectable loss of specificity or within-family predictive ability.

papers.title: Accelerometry-Derived REM Sleep Behavior Disorder Score Is Associated with Incident Parkinson's Disease in the UK Biobank
papers.abstract: Estimating Parkinson's disease (PD) risk years before diagnosis remains an unmet need. We applied a validated machine learning classifier for REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) detection to 7-day wrist accelerometry data in 87,975 UK Biobank participants followed for 10 years. Participants in the highest RBD risk stratum (>99th percentile) had an approximately fivefold increased hazard of incident PD compared with the lowest-risk group (0-90th percentile), with a dose-dependent relationship across the full score distribution. Among non-converters, higher RBD-classifier scores were associated with baseline cognitive deficits and greater burden of autonomic and psychiatric prodromal features. The association with incident PD remained independent of PD polygenic risk score, while RBD-classifier score and genetic risk were synergistic. The combined high-risk group achieved a positive likelihood ratio of 7.91, approximately threefold higher than questionnaire-based RBD screening. At this High-risk threshold over the 10-year horizon, the classifier showed a sensitivity of 7.4%, specificity of 99.2%, positive predictive value of 7.5%, and negative predictive value of 99.2% for incident PD (N=50,816). These findings support wrist accelerometry as a scalable, high-specificity approach for prodromal PD risk enrichment.
